title: Word Embeddings
oneLineScope: Dense learned word vectors: word2vec and GloVe, and the analogy arithmetic that surprised everyone.
prose:
Where we are. The previous node built a semantic geometry out of raw co-occurrence counts: apply PPMI weighting, factor with SVD, and Harris’s distributional hypothesis materializes as a spatial arrangement of word vectors. That pipeline works, but it is a two-stage affair — count, then factorize — and the resulting vectors are tied to a fixed vocabulary and awkward to slot into a gradient-based system. A natural question follows: can you get the same kind of vectors, or better ones, by training for them directly? This node is the answer.

The gist. Word2vec and GloVe replace the count-then-factorize pipeline with learned dense vectors — embeddings: fixed-dimensional real-valued representations of discrete word types, trained end-to-end from a prediction objective. Word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) trains a deliberately shallow network to predict which words appear near each other; the learned weight matrices become the word vectors. GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014) returns to the global co-occurrence matrix but fits it with a weighted least-squares objective rather than algebraic SVD. Both produce vectors where semantic and syntactic relations appear as geometric structure — the famous analogy arithmetic — and both, it turns out, are performing a kind of low-rank matrix factorization of co-occurrence statistics. The theoretical circle closes: these are the distributional hypothesis, implemented by gradient descent.

Why it matters. These embeddings are the input representation that every architecture downstream depends on. When a transformer “takes tokens as input,” what it actually receives is a row lookup into an embedding matrix; this node is where that matrix comes from. But these vectors are static: one fixed vector per word type, blind to context. That is the limitation attention later removes — scaled dot-product attention transforms a static embedding into a context-sensitive representation by conditioning it on the rest of the sequence. Understanding what embeddings are and what they cannot do is the prerequisite for understanding why attention is necessary.

The embedding matrix

The data structure first. Fix a vocabulary of \(V\) word types. An embedding matrix \(E \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times d}\) assigns each type a row vector of dimension \(d\) — the embedding dimension, a hyperparameter, typically 100–300 for word2vec-era models. The integer index of a word (its position in the vocabulary list) selects its row by lookup; an embedding is simply a learned parameter table. During training, gradient descent updates every row that is “looked up” in a given batch and leaves the rest unchanged. At convergence, those rows are the word vectors.

word2vec: learning from prediction

Mikolov et al. (2013) introduced two shallow architectures under the word2vec umbrella. The motivating intuition is the same for both: instead of counting co-occurrences and then factorizing, train a network to predict which words tend to appear together, and harvest the word vectors from the weight matrices that form in that process. The co-occurrence signal is the same as Harris’s; the optimization path is different.

CBOW (Continuous Bag of Words) predicts a center word from the average of its context words’ embeddings — a fast, smoothed model that handles frequent words well.

Skip-gram reverses the direction: given a center word \(w_{\text{center}}\), predict each surrounding context word \(w_{\text{ctx}}\) within a window of size \(m\). The training objective is to maximize the log-likelihood over all (center, context) pairs in the corpus:

\[ \mathcal{L} = \sum_{\text{pairs}} \log p(w_{\text{ctx}} \mid w_{\text{center}}) \]

where \(p(w_{\text{ctx}} \mid w_{\text{center}})\) is a softmax over the entire vocabulary:

\[ p(w_{\text{ctx}} \mid w_{\text{center}}) = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{e}_{\text{center}} \cdot \mathbf{e}'_{\text{ctx}})}{\sum_{v=1}^{V} \exp(\mathbf{e}_{\text{center}} \cdot \mathbf{e}'_v)} \]

Here \(\mathbf{e}_{\text{center}} \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is the center word’s row in the input embedding matrix \(E\), and \(\mathbf{e}'_{\text{ctx}} \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is the context word’s row in a second, output embedding matrix \(E' \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times d}\). Two separate matrices for input and output roles are standard practice; after training, the input matrix \(E\) is used as the word embeddings. There is no hidden layer between them — the network is deliberately shallow, which keeps training tractable at large vocabulary sizes.

Negative sampling: making the softmax tractable

The full-vocabulary softmax in the denominator above sums over \(V\) terms for every training example. With \(V = 10^5\)–\(10^6\), this is prohibitive. The practical solution, introduced in Mikolov et al. (2013b), is negative sampling: replace the softmax with a binary discrimination problem. For each true (center, context) pair, sample \(k\) “negative” context words at random from a noise distribution \(P_n\) (the unigram distribution raised to the \(3/4\) power, which moderately undersamples very frequent words). The objective becomes:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{NEG}} = \log \sigma(\mathbf{e}_{\text{center}} \cdot \mathbf{e}'_{\text{ctx}}) + \sum_{i=1}^{k} \mathbb{E}_{w_i \sim P_n}\left[ \log \sigma(-\mathbf{e}_{\text{center}} \cdot \mathbf{e}'_{w_i}) \right] \]

where \(\sigma\) is the logistic function. You can recognize this as noise-contrastive estimation (NCE): the model learns to distinguish true co-occurrences from noise-generated pairs, and the log-likelihood of the true pair relative to the noise pairs is maximized. The statistical framing is sound: NCE approximates the full softmax at a fraction of the computational cost, and with \(k = 5\)–\(20\) negatives it recovers nearly the same quality vectors. This is the practical trick that made word2vec fast enough to train on billions of tokens on a single machine.

GloVe: count-based, but still learned

Pennington, Socher, and Manning (2014) returned to the count-matrix perspective with GloVe (Global Vectors for Word Representation). Rather than predicting local context windows, GloVe trains on the global word–word co-occurrence matrix \(X_{\text{co}} \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times V}\) computed over the full corpus, where entry \((X_{\text{co}})_{ij}\) counts how many times word \(j\) appears in the context of word \(i\). The objective fits a weighted least-squares criterion:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{GloVe}} = \sum_{i,j=1}^{V} f\bigl((X_{\text{co}})_{ij}\bigr) \left( \mathbf{e}_i \cdot \mathbf{e}'_j + b_i + b'_j - \log (X_{\text{co}})_{ij} \right)^2 \]

where \(f(\cdot)\) is a weighting function that down-weights very common co-occurrences, \(b_i\) and \(b'_j\) are scalar bias terms, and the objective asks the dot product of the two embedding vectors to approximate the log co-occurrence count. The explicit connection back to Harris and the PPMI matrix of the previous node is deliberate: GloVe makes the factorization explicit and optimizes it directly with gradient descent rather than algebraic SVD.

Empirically, word2vec (predictive, local windows) and GloVe (count-based, global matrix) produce vectors of comparable quality on most benchmarks. The theoretical gap is smaller than the architectural difference suggests: Levy & Goldberg (2014) showed that skip-gram with negative sampling implicitly factorizes a shifted PMI matrix, so both methods are, at bottom, low-rank factorizations of co-occurrence statistics, differing mainly in which statistics they privilege and how the optimization proceeds. The choice between them is largely empirical.

Analogy arithmetic

The result that caught everyone’s attention was not retrieval quality but geometry. Mikolov et al. observed that simple vector arithmetic on the learned representations could recover semantic and syntactic relations. The most-cited example:

\(\mathbf{e}_{\text{king}} - \mathbf{e}_{\text{man}} + \mathbf{e}_{\text{woman}} \approx \mathbf{e}_{\text{queen}}\)

The vector offset from man to king is approximately equal to the offset from woman to queen. The same parallelogram structure appears for capital–country pairs (Paris − France + Italy ≈ Rome), verb tenses (walked − walk + swim ≈ swam), and comparative adjectives.

The explanation is distributional and not mysterious. If king and man share all their masculine co-occurrence contexts and differ mainly in their regal ones, and queen and woman share all their feminine contexts and differ in the same regal ones, then a training procedure that encodes co-occurrence structure geometrically will place all four words such that the royalty direction is consistent. The relational structure emerges from the optimization, not from any explicit encoding.

The honest caveat: the effect is sensitive to the specific word pairs, the training corpus, the dimensionality \(d\), and normalization choices. Accuracy on Mikolov et al.’s standard analogy benchmark ranges from roughly 40% to 75% depending on these factors. Results are often cherry-picked in presentations. The phenomenon is real but should be understood as a statistical tendency, not a reliable algebraic identity; later work by Linzen (2016) and others showed the effect can disappear for less canonical pairs.

The fundamental limitation: static representations

Both word2vec and GloVe produce static embeddings: one fixed vector per word type, regardless of context. Bank in “river bank” and bank in “central bank” map to exactly the same row of \(E\) at inference time. This is the same limitation identified at the end of the previous node for LSA: the distributional hypothesis is satisfied in expectation over all contexts, but individual occurrences are not distinguished. The vector for bank is a superposition of financial and geographical senses, compressed into a single point.

The remedy requires making representations contextual — computing a fresh representation for each token occurrence from its actual surroundings rather than from a fixed lookup. Word embeddings are the starting point, the initial \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_{\text{model}}}\) fed to the transformer (one row per token position). Scaled dot-product attention is the mechanism that transforms those static rows into context-sensitive representations by letting each position attend to the rest of the sequence. What comes out of each attention layer is something the embedding matrix alone cannot produce: a vector for bank that reflects which sense is active in this sentence.

diagrams.caption: Skip-gram architecture: a center word is looked up in the V×d input embedding matrix, producing a d-dimensional vector that is scored against the output embedding matrix to predict context words. Negative sampling replaces the full-vocabulary softmax with k+1 binary logistic decisions.
diagrams.altText: A left-to-right pipeline. On the left, a box labeled center word (integer index) feeds into a box labeled input embedding matrix E, shape V by d, via an arrow labeled lookup. The lookup extracts a single row vector labeled e_center, shape 1 by d. That vector feeds into a box labeled output embedding matrix E-prime, shape V by d, via a multiply arrow, producing a score vector of shape 1 by V. A note reads: full softmax over V is intractable. An arrow leads to a box labeled negative sampling: 1 true context word plus k noise words, logistic loss. The output on the right is labeled updated embeddings.
diagrams.prompt: Structural data-flow diagram, left to right, of the skip-gram word2vec architecture with negative sampling. Start on the left with a small box labeled 'center word (index)'. An arrow labeled 'lookup' leads into a tall rectangle labeled 'E (input embeddings)' with shape annotation 'V × d'; a highlighted row is extracted from it, drawn as a thin rectangle labeled 'e_center' with shape '1 × d'. An arrow from e_center labeled '× E′ (output embeddings, V × d)' leads to a score vector of shape '1 × V'. Below the score vector, add a note: 'full softmax over V: intractable (V ≈ 10⁵)'. An arrow leads into a box labeled 'negative sampling' containing: '1 true context pair (logistic +)' and 'k noise-sampled words (logistic −)'. The final output on the right is labeled 'gradient → update E rows'. Label every matrix with its name and shape. Mark V × d on both E and E′. Keep it clean and structural.

diagrams.caption: Analogy arithmetic as parallel vector offsets: the offset from man to king is the same as the offset from woman to queen, illustrating that the embedding space encodes the gender–royalty relation as a consistent direction.
diagrams.altText: A 2-D coordinate space with four labeled points: man and woman in the lower region, king and queen in the upper region. Arrows connect man to king and woman to queen, both pointing in the same upper-right direction and labeled with the same offset delta. A dashed arrow from king minus man plus woman points to queen. A note reads: vector arithmetic recovers relational structure — but effect is sensitive to corpus and parameters.
diagrams.prompt: Conceptual diagram showing word embedding analogy arithmetic as a parallelogram in 2-D space. Draw a 2-D coordinate space (axes lightly sketched, unlabeled). Place four labeled word points: 'man' (lower-left), 'woman' (lower-right), 'king' (upper-left), 'queen' (upper-right), arranged as the four corners of a rough parallelogram. Draw an arrow from man to king, labeled 'royalty offset'. Draw an arrow from woman to queen, labeled the same offset, both arrows parallel and approximately equal in length. Draw a dashed arrow from the tip of (king − man + woman) to queen, labeled 'king − man + woman ≈ queen'. Add a short margin note: 'offsets encode relations — but effect is corpus- and parameter-sensitive'. No equations beyond the label; this is the intuition diagram.

bibliography.citation: Mikolov, T., Chen, K., Corrado, G., & Dean, J. (2013). Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space. arXiv:1301.3781.
bibliography.annotation: The original word2vec paper. Introduces both CBOW and skip-gram architectures and reports the analogy evaluation results. §2 defines the models; §3 describes the training; §4.2 is the analogy task. The paper is short and worth reading directly.

bibliography.citation: Mikolov, T., Sutskever, I., Chen, K., Corrado, G., & Dean, J. (2013). Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality. NeurIPS. arXiv:1310.4546.
bibliography.annotation: The negative-sampling paper. §2.2 introduces the negative-sampling objective and the noise distribution; §2.3 explains subsampling of frequent words. This is the practical version of word2vec most implementations actually use. The NCE connection is discussed in the appendix.

bibliography.citation: Pennington, J., Socher, R., & Manning, C. D. (2014). GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation. EMNLP.
bibliography.annotation: The GloVe paper. §2 derives the weighted least-squares objective from co-occurrence statistics; §3 justifies the log co-occurrence target. The comparison to skip-gram in §4 is useful for understanding where the two approaches converge and diverge.

Visual walk-through of the skip-gram training process, negative sampling, and the resulting embedding geometry. Complements the formal papers well; particularly useful for the intuition behind what the network is actually learning step by step.
